source: NYC Zoning Resolution, Articles II, III and IV, as amended by City of Yes (2024)
note: The 2024 City of Yes amendment replaced the old numbered Use Groups 1 through 18 with ten Roman numeral Use Groups. Old Use Groups 10 and 12 were eliminated.

L.label: Permitted with limitations
L.desc: Allowed as of right only in some cases, limited by district or geography.

S.label: Special permit required
S.desc: Allowed only with approval from the Board of Standards and Appeals or the City Planning Commission.

flags.S: Size restriction, such as a floor area or capacity cap
flags.P: Additional conditions, such as environmental or location standards
flags.U: Open use allowance, meaning the use need not be enclosed

R.name: Residence
R.desc: Where people live. R1 and R2 are the lowest density, largely detached houses. R6 and above allow apartment buildings, and R9 through R12 are the densest. Retail is generally not permitted in a Residence District, which is why commercial overlays exist.

C.name: Commercial
C.desc: C1 and C2 are overlays mapped on top of Residence Districts for local retail. C3 is waterfront recreation. C4 is regional shopping outside the central business districts. C5 and C6 are the central business districts. C7 is large open amusement. C8 is heavy service and automotive, the only Commercial District where housing is not allowed.

M.name: Manufacturing
M.desc: M1 is light manufacturing with performance standards limiting noise, odor and emissions. M2 is medium. M3 is heavy industrial, for uses with the greatest nuisance potential, generally on the waterfront. Housing is not permitted as of right in Manufacturing Districts except in paired MX districts and certain special districts.

groups.name: Agriculture and Open Uses
groups.plain: Land used mostly in the open rather than inside a building.
examples: Outdoor racket courts and skating rinks

R.note: Parks and golf courses are permitted in every Residence District. Cemeteries are not permitted in R1 or R2. Outdoor racket courts and skating rinks need a special permit in R1 and R2, and are permitted with conditions elsewhere. Sand, gravel or clay pits always require a special permit.

C.note: Parks, cemeteries, golf courses, racket courts and skating rinks are permitted in every Commercial District. Agricultural uses carry size limits in C1 and C2. Sand, gravel or clay pits always require a special permit.

M.note: Generally permitted. See Article IV for the district by district table.

groups.name: Residences
groups.plain: Places people live, from single family houses to apartment buildings.
examples: Single family homes, detached or attached

R.note: This is the core of what a Residence District is for. R1 and R2 are limited to single family detached homes unless the lot is a qualifying residential site. R3, R4 and R5 have their own limits by subdistrict, for example R4B allows single and two family homes detached, semi detached, attached or zero lot line. R6 through R12 allow all residence types including apartment buildings.

C.note: Permitted in C1, C2, C5 and C6 without special limitation. C3 is limited to single or two family detached or zero lot line homes in C3A. C4 allows all residential uses with a Staten Island exception. Housing is NOT permitted in C7 or C8.

M.note: Not permitted as of right in Manufacturing Districts, other than in paired MX districts, certain M1 subdistricts and special purpose districts. This is the single biggest constraint on converting industrial land to housing.

groups.name: Community Facilities
groups.plain: Uses that provide educational, religious, health and other essential services. Split into those with sleeping accommodations and those without.
examples: Hospitals and long term care facilities
Ambulatory diagnostic or treatment health care facilities
Libraries, museums, non commercial art galleries

R.note: Schools, houses of worship, libraries, museums, hospitals and community centers are permitted in every Residence District. In R1 and R2 several uses need a special permit: dormitories, colleges, non commercial clubs and welfare centers. Ambulatory health care facilities are not permitted in R1 or R2 at all, and are size limited in R3 and R4.

C.note: Permitted across C1 through C7. C8 is the exception: no dormitories, no colleges, no libraries or museums, no long term care, and schools only by special permit.

M.note: Permitted with significant limits, varying by district and by whether the facility has sleeping accommodations. See Article IV.

groups.name: Public Service Facilities and Infrastructure
groups.plain: Public services and the physical infrastructure the city runs on.
examples: Fire and police stations, court houses
Docks, railroad rights of way, transit substations
Energy infrastructure equipment, solar and battery

R.note: Most infrastructure requires a special permit in Residence Districts, including fire and police stations, utility substations and sewage plants. Railroad rights of way and energy infrastructure equipment are permitted as of right. Power plants, waste transfer stations, incinerators, airports, bus stations, freight terminals and prisons are never permitted.

C.note: Court houses and fire and police stations are permitted in most Commercial Districts but not C3. Utility substations are permitted with size limits. Prisons are permitted in C4 through C8. Power plants, composting, dumps, incinerators, airports and truck weighing stations are never permitted.

M.note: Manufacturing Districts are where the heaviest infrastructure is allowed, including power plants, waste transfer, and freight terminals, subject to district and performance standards. See Article IV.

groups.name: Transient Accommodations
groups.plain: Places to stay temporarily rather than live.

R.note: Effectively not available. Overnight camps require a special permit from the Board of Standards and Appeals. Transient hotels are only possible in R10H Districts, and only by special permit of the City Planning Commission.

C.note: Since December 2021, a transient hotel anywhere in a Commercial District requires a special permit from the City Planning Commission for new development, conversion, or a 20 percent or greater enlargement. Hotels existing on 9 December 2021 are conforming and may continue. Not permitted in C3. In C1 and C2 overlays, limited to sites within 1,000 feet of a highway ramp.

M.note: Also subject to the 2021 hotel special permit requirement in most cases. See Article IV.

groups.name: Retail and Services
groups.plain: Uses where goods or services are conveyed directly to consumers. This is the storefront use group.
examples: Grocery, specialty food, beer wine and liquor retailers
Clothing, shoe, jewelry, book and hobby retailers
Banks, real estate, insurance and professional services
Barbers, salons, laundry and dry cleaning
Motor vehicle dealers and repair, car washes

R.note: Not permitted in Residence Districts. This is the fundamental reason for C1 and C2 commercial overlays: they are mapped on top of Residence Districts specifically to allow local retail on a corner or an avenue.

C.note: The defining use group of Commercial Districts, but heavily graded. C1 and C2 carry floor area caps per establishment, often 10,000 square feet, and 3,000 in select commercial overlays. C3 allows almost nothing except specialty food, sporting goods and eating or drinking. Automotive repair, car washes, industrial laundry and fuel dealers are largely confined to C8.

M.note: Widely permitted, often without the size caps that apply in C1 and C2. See Article IV.

groups.name: Offices and Laboratories
groups.plain: Administrative and research workspace for business, professional or governmental purposes.
examples: Ambulatory diagnostic or treatment health care offices

R.note: Effectively not available. Laboratories require a special permit of the City Planning Commission. Ground floor offices are only possible within the flood zone by special permit of the Board of Standards and Appeals.

C.note: Offices are permitted in every Commercial District except C3. Laboratories are permitted subject to Building Code standards, and are not permitted in C1 select commercial overlays outside Manhattan.

groups.name: Recreation, Entertainment and Assembly Spaces
groups.plain: Places people gather for recreation, entertainment or assembly.
examples: Art galleries and art, music, dance or theatrical studios
Meeting halls and non commercial clubs
Observation decks and publicly accessible spaces
Outdoor day camps, riding academies and stables

R.note: Effectively not available. Only outdoor day camps and riding academies or stables, and both require a special permit from the Board of Standards and Appeals.

C.note: Broadly permitted in C4 through C8. In C1 and C2 amusement and entertainment facilities are size capped, often 10,000 square feet and 3,000 in select overlays. Arenas, auditoriums, stadiums and trade expositions are capped at 2,500 seats or persons without a City Planning Commission special permit. C3 allows very little. Drive in theaters and racetracks need special permits and only in C7 or C8.

M.note: Generally permitted, and the districts where the largest venues are possible. See Article IV.

groups.name: Storage
groups.plain: Storage of materials, goods and vehicles. Split into general storage, specialized storage and vehicle storage.
examples: Trucking terminals and motor freight stations
Junk or salvage yards, petroleum storage, grain storage

C.note: Sharply limited. Warehouses, self service storage, moving offices, trucking terminals and building material yards are C8 only. Micro distribution is capped at 2,500 square feet in C1 and C2 and 5,000 on the ground floor in C4 through C7. All specialized storage, including junk yards, petroleum, grain, coal and scrap metal, is not permitted in any Commercial District. Public parking garages are limited by capacity and by whether the district is in the Greater Transit Zone.

M.note: This is where the storage uses barred from Commercial Districts are allowed, including specialized storage in M2 and M3. See Article IV.

groups.name: Production Uses
groups.plain: Uses engaged in the mechanical, physical or chemical transformation of materials into new goods.
examples: Computer, electronic and medical equipment manufacturing

C.note: Light production is permitted in most Commercial Districts, a significant change from the old rules, but with hard size caps: 3,000 square feet in C1 select overlays, 5,000 in other C1 and C2, and 10,000 on the ground floor in C4 through C7. All must meet M1 performance standards. Heavier production, including slaughtering, tanning, distilling, petroleum, plastics, primary metals and transportation equipment, is not permitted in any Commercial District.

M.note: The core purpose of Manufacturing Districts. M1 requires the strictest performance standards, M3 the loosest. See Article IV.

misconception.t: The letter is a name, not a description
misconception.b: R does not mean only housing. C does not mean no housing. M does not mean only factories. The letter tells you which set of rules applies to the lot, not what is actually allowed on it. Every district type permits several Use Groups, and the surprises run in both directions.

cards.name: Residence
cards.truth: Housing plus community facilities as of right: schools, houses of worship, libraries, museums, hospitals, community centers and non profit institutions. Parks and agricultural uses too, and railroad rights of way and energy infrastructure. What R actually excludes is retail, storage and production.
cards.eg: 250 Baltic Street is zoned R6 and contains a public library and a government office, not a single apartment.

cards.name: Commercial
cards.truth: Housing is permitted as of right in C1, C2, C4, C5 and C6, and limited in C3. Most of the housing in New York City sits in a Commercial District or under a commercial overlay. Only C7 and C8 exclude residences. Community facilities are permitted across almost all of them, and light production is now allowed under size caps.
cards.eg: A C1-3 or C2-4 overlay on a residential avenue is still a Commercial District, and the apartments above the shops are entirely legal.

cards.name: Manufacturing
cards.truth: Offices, retail and services, storage, entertainment venues and most infrastructure are permitted, often with fewer size limits than in a Commercial District. Community facilities are permitted with restrictions. The one thing M districts bar as of right is housing, and even that has an exception: a paired MX district written as M1-4/R6A permits residential and light industrial together on the same lot.
cards.eg: An office, a gym, a brewery taproom and a theater can all be as of right in an M1 District. And in Gowanus, an M1-4/R6A lot permits apartments and light manufacturing at once.

misconception.close: This matters in practice because people argue about the letter rather than the Use Group. If someone says a use does not belong because the lot is zoned R, the useful question is which Use Group the use falls into and whether that Use Group is permitted there. Very often it is.

changing.t: Changing the use is administrative only if the new use is already permitted
changing.lead: The qualifier is the whole point, and it is where people go wrong in both directions. If the use you want is permitted in that zoning district, switching to it is a filing with the Department of Buildings: no rezoning, no Board of Standards and Appeals, no community board vote, no hearing. If it is not permitted, none of that applies and there is no administrative route at all. The same physical change to the same building is either routine paperwork or a multi-year public process, and which one it is depends entirely on whether the Use Group is allowed there.

paths.b: The owner files with the Department of Buildings for a new or amended Certificate of Occupancy. DOB checks that the proposed use is permitted in the zoning district and that the building meets the Building Code for that occupancy, which can mean real work on egress, sprinklers, accessibility and exiting. That is a plan examination, not a land use review.
paths.review: No public review. No community board vote. No hearing.
paths.eg: A ground floor retail space in a C1 overlay becoming a restaurant. Both are Use Group VI. An office becoming a medical office. Both are Use Group VII. A church hall becoming a day care. Both are Use Group III.

paths.t: The use is not permitted and the owner wants relief on this lot
paths.b: A use variance from the Board of Standards and Appeals. The applicant must prove all five statutory findings, including that the lot cannot yield a reasonable return under any permitted use, that the hardship is unique to the lot, that the character of the neighborhood will not be altered, that the hardship was not self created, and that the variance is the minimum necessary. This is a genuinely high bar.
paths.review: Public hearing. The community board has 45 days to submit a written recommendation. Advisory, but it goes in the record.
paths.eg: A use that the zoning simply does not allow on that lot, where the owner argues the lot cannot work otherwise.

paths.t: The zoning contemplates the use but requires discretion
paths.b: A special permit from the Board of Standards and Appeals or the City Planning Commission, depending on which the Zoning Resolution names. Unlike a variance, the zoning text already anticipates the use and sets the findings. The applicant must meet those findings rather than prove hardship.
paths.review: Public hearing. The community board reviews and votes.
paths.eg: A transient hotel in a Commercial District. An arena above 2,500 seats. An eating and drinking establishment over 200 capacity near a Residence District boundary.

paths.b: A zoning map amendment, which is a ULURP action. The clock starts when City Planning certifies the application. The community board has 60 days including a public hearing and a vote, then the Borough President has 30 days, the City Planning Commission 60, the City Council 50, and the Mayor 5 days to sign or veto. This is the only path that changes what is permitted for everyone on the lot and often the block, permanently.
paths.who: City Planning Commission and City Council
paths.review: Full ULURP. Community board public hearing and vote.
paths.eg: Converting a manufacturing district to allow residential use. The Gowanus rezoning is the local example.

changing.why: The practical consequence is that a great deal of change people expect to have a say over is not reviewable at all. If a use is as of right, the community board learns about it when the permit appears, not before. That is not an oversight in the system, it is the design: zoning decides once, in public, what is allowed, and after that owners may use their property within those rules without asking again. The moment for public input is the rezoning, not the tenant.
changing.flag: Worth checking before objecting: if a proposed use is already permitted, there is no application to oppose and no body with jurisdiction to stop it. Time is better spent on whether the underlying zoning is right.

steps: What Use Group is the proposed use in?
Every use falls into one of the ten Use Groups. That is the unit the Zoning Resolution works in, not the business name or the signage.
Is that Use Group permitted in this zoning district?
Check the district, and check any commercial overlay, which can permit uses the base district does not. This is the question that decides everything after it.
If yes, is it within the size and location limits?

Many permitted uses carry caps: floor area per establishment, capacity, distance from a Residence District boundary. Inside the limits it stays administrative. Outside them it becomes a special permit.
Only if the answer to 2 is no do you reach BSA or ULURP.
A use the zoning does not permit cannot be filed for administratively at any size. That is when a variance or a rezoning is the only path.

changing.warn: Two mistakes follow from missing the qualifier. The first is assuming every new tenant is reviewable, and objecting to something no agency has jurisdiction to stop. The second is assuming any use can be swapped in administratively, which is how owners end up filing for something that was never permitted and getting stopped at plan examination. The Use Group and the district together decide which situation you are in.

districtword.lead: District is one of the most overloaded words in New York City civic life. It means at least six different things depending on who is speaking, the boundaries almost never line up, and people routinely argue past each other because they are each talking about a different one.

kinds.d: A mapped area with one set of rules about what may be built and how big. This is the only kind of district on this page. It is drawn on the zoning map, and changing it requires a rezoning through ULURP.
One of 59 areas, each served by a community board. It is the geography this site is organised around. A community district contains many zoning districts.
One of 51 electoral districts. The member representing it holds the deciding vote on most rezonings in it, which is why it matters to land use even though it is an electoral boundary.
An area designated for its architectural or historic character. It governs what buildings look like, not what they may be used for, and it sits entirely outside the zoning map.

kinds.w: Special Gowanus Mixed Use District, Special Battery Park City District
kinds.d: A district created in the Zoning Resolution that writes its own rules for a defined area, replacing or modifying what the ordinary district would allow. The 2021 Gowanus rezoning created one here in Community District 6, pairing manufacturing and residential districts on the same lots. Battery Park City has another, subdivided into Zone A residential, Zone B commercial office core and Zone C mixed. Inside one of these the ordinary Use Group tables are not the controlling text.
Each agency draws its own service areas for its own operational reasons. None of them affect what can be built anywhere.

districtword.close: None of these boundaries are required to match, and mostly they do not. A single lot sits inside a zoning district, a community district, a council district, a school district, a police precinct and possibly a historic district and a special purpose district, all at once, each drawn by a different body for a different purpose. When someone says a proposal is wrong for the district, the first useful question is which district they mean.

options.t: It is not permitted. What are the options?
options.lead: There are five, and they are not interchangeable. They differ in who decides, how long it takes, what it changes, and how hard it is to win. Picking the wrong one wastes years.

list.n: Do something else that is permitted
list.time: Weeks to months, DOB filing only
list.odds: Certain, if the use is permitted
list.when: Almost always worth checking first. Use Groups are broad, and a related use often falls in a permitted group. A medical office and a business office are both Use Group VII. A day care and a school are both Use Group III.
for: No public process, no hearing, no waiting
No legal or consultant cost of any consequence
Cannot be denied if the use is genuinely permitted
against: Only works if what you want can be reshaped into a permitted use
Does not help if the use itself is the point

list.who: Board of Standards and Appeals, five members appointed by the Mayor
list.odds: Low. The five findings are a genuinely high bar
list.scope: This lot only. It does not change the zoning for anyone else
list.when: When the lot itself has a problem no permitted use can overcome, such as an unusual shape, topography or subsurface condition.
for: Does not require changing the zoning map
Confined to the lot, so it does not set a precedent for the block
Community board reviews but the decision is the BSA's
against: All five findings must be proven, including that no permitted use can yield a reasonable return
The hardship cannot be self created, which rules out having overpaid for the site
Expensive: needs a zoning attorney, an appraiser and often an engineer
Financial hardship alone is never enough

list.who: BSA or the City Planning Commission, whichever the Zoning Resolution names
list.time: Under a year at the BSA, longer at CPC
list.odds: Moderate. The findings are written down and can be met
list.when: When the Zoning Resolution already contemplates the use in that district but requires discretion. This only exists where the text says so.
for: The findings are set out in the text rather than requiring proof of hardship
A far lower bar than a variance
Predictable: you can read what you have to show
against: Only available where the Zoning Resolution provides for it
Still a public hearing with community board review
Conditions can be attached to the approval

list.who: City Planning Commission and City Council, initiated by an applicant or the city
list.time: About seven months once certified, plus a pre-certification period that commonly runs a year or more
list.odds: Depends almost entirely on the local Council Member
list.scope: Everyone in the rezoned area, permanently
list.when: When the district itself is wrong for the area, not just for one lot. Gowanus is the local example.
for: Changes what is permitted as of right, so no further approvals are needed afterwards
Can be paired with commitments on affordability and infrastructure
The only path that fixes the problem for the whole area
against: The full ULURP clock: community board 60 days with a hearing and vote, Borough President 30, City Planning Commission 60, City Council 50, Mayor 5
Member deference means the local Council Member effectively decides
Expensive and slow, with environmental review often the longest part
Changes the rules for neighbours who did not ask for it

list.who: City Planning Commission and City Council
list.time: Comparable to a map amendment, often longer
list.odds: Low for a single applicant, higher when the city initiates it
list.scope: Every lot the text touches, which can be citywide
list.when: When the rule itself is the problem rather than where the line is drawn. City of Yes was a text amendment.
for: Fixes a category of problem rather than one site
Can be initiated by the city rather than a private applicant
against: Rarely viable for one applicant with one site
Broadest possible opposition, since it affects everyone

options.advice: The order above is roughly the order to consider them. Most people jump to the rezoning because it is the one they have heard of, when the first option resolves the situation more often than not. Before spending anything, the question worth answering is whether the thing you actually want is already permitted under a Use Group you had not thought to check.
options.cb: Whichever path applies, the community board is in it. On a variance or special permit the board reviews and submits a recommendation. On a ULURP action the board holds a public hearing and votes within 60 days. The vote is advisory in every case, but it is on the record and it carries weight, particularly where there is pressure from more than one direction.
